newsitem.title: USA: Six Viper militia sentenced to prison in Arizona.
newsitem.headline: Six Viper militia sentenced to prison in Arizona.

text.p: Six members of the self-styled Viper Militia, arrested in a series of raids by anti-terrorist agents last year, were sentenced Wednesday to jail terms for conspiracy to make bombs.
"There was never any intention to harm anyone; there was no plan," one of the six, Donna Williams, told the court as she broke down in tears.
Another militia member, David Belliveau, told Federal Judge Earl Carroll: "I feel very bad, guilty. (I) used very poor judgment."

At the time of their arrest last July, President Clinton said "a terrible terrorist attack" had been averted, but prosecutors later said there was no indication the suspects were planning any specific attacks.
Defence lawyers characterised the suspects as gun enthusiasts who went to remote desert areas of Arizona to "blow up dirt."

Videotapes seized at the time of their arrests and later shown in court depicted several members firing guns and setting off explosions in remote areas. Agents also seized manuals on bomb-making and maps pointing out federal and state buildings in the Phoenix area.

Some of those arrested also were in possession of machine guns and quantities of ammonium nitrate -- a chemical common in fertilisers. The chemical can be used to manufacture explosives and was a component of the deadly bomb that devastated a federal building in Oklahoma City in 1995.
The six sentenced Wednesday had all pleaded guilty in an agreement with federal prosecutors. Four of their fellow paramilitary militia members were to be sentenced later.
Two more Viper militiamen have pleaded not guilty and their trial is set to start March 25.
All six sentenced by Judge Carroll in Phoenix Wednesday were put on three years probation and directed not to associate with any paramilitary or militia groups.
Belliveau, his wife Ellen, Williams, Henry Overturf, Walter Sanville and Scott Shero were all convicted of conspiracy to manufacture and possess destructive devices.
Sanville, 37, was also convicted on two counts of unlawful possession of machine guns. He was jailed for 37 months and fined $2,800.
Overturf, 37, and Williams, 44, were each jailed for 12 months and one day and fined $1,600, while Shero, 31, received a 24-month prison term and a $1,600 fine.

David Belliveau, 28, was sentenced to 57 months and fined $300. He was convicted of a further count of conspiracy to furnish instruction in the use of explosive devices in the furtherance of civil disorder and a count of unlawful possession of a machine gun.
Ellen Belliveau, 27, was also convicted of the instruction count and received a 37-month term and $200 fine.
Her lawyer Marty Lieberman told the judge: "I think she got swept up in the rhetoric -- this became Ellen's extended family."
